title: The Ode in Praise of Ali
intro: Husayn Abu al-Faraj wrote this ode for Ali ibn Abi Talib. Alqimmah Studio released Khalid al-Sharafi's recitation in 2023, with section announcements by Riyad al-Nu'man. From the desert of time separating the speaker from Ali, the poem moves through Ali's ancestry and family, his life with Muhammad, and the civil wars of his caliphate. It takes a Sunni view of the first civil war and occasionally names a transmitter whose account it follows, as it does for Ali's pledge to Abu Bakr. After recounting Ali's death, the poet turns to the listener and asks what it means to follow a man one loves.

translation: I walk proudly, exulting among people,
for I fashion pearls in praise of Ali.
1.sharh: The speaker's pride comes from the person he celebrates. He imagines each word as a pearl that takes work to set.

translation: To the noble father of Hasan and Husayn they set out,
the caravans of praise, with reverence singing them on.
2.sharh: Praises become caravans travelling to Ali. Reverence takes the camel driver's place and sings to keep them moving.

translation: Between us lie deserts whose sand is ages,
and awe as vast, beyond anyone's power to match.
3.sharh: Centuries stretch out like grains of desert sand. Awe places the speaker just as far from the man he addresses.

translation: I know what hardship the journey holds,
but I have a purpose in making it.
4.sharh: He chooses the journey with its hardships in view. The repeated words for travelling and intending give his undertaking the weight of a deliberate act.

translation: You are more to us than stories of times gone by.
Your warning rings truest in whatever comes anew.
5.sharh: Ali's life speaks to new events. A story about the past can still tell the listener what to look for in the present.

translation: Your conduct and the traces you left preach more powerfully
than sermons called forth by every need.
6.sharh: Example has an eloquence of its own. Ali's conduct in life and the record it left can move a listener more deeply than an expressly delivered sermon.

translation: Your verse and your speeches are more eloquent
than all that wells from native masters' mouths.
7.sharh: Even people whose eloquence wells up naturally cannot, in the poet's estimation, match Ali in either verse or public speech.

translation: You are braver when the horsemen charge
and their seasoned mounts bring them to death's watering place.
8.sharh: A watering place ordinarily sustains rider and horse. Here the horses bear their riders to a place where they may die.

translation: You are closer in blood to the Chosen One,
and his daughter is your wife, your affection freely shared.
9.sharh: Ali is both Muhammad's cousin and his son-in-law. The second half brings the family relationship down to the affection between husband and wife.

translation: In you alone among the Companions lies a test
of people's souls, of those who go too far and those who hate.
10.sharh: Two almost identical Arabic words name opposite responses to Ali, excessive veneration and aversion. Both fall outside the affection the poet advocates.

translation: Abu Turab, by God, our hearts have drunk in love.
We water them with the traditions we tell.
11.sharh: Narrated traditions keep love alive. The Arabic verb for watering also evokes the telling of a report, so the hearts drink what the narrators pass on.

translation: We honour our love for God's Messenger
in his pure family, for whom we would give our fathers.
12.sharh: Love for Muhammad entails a duty towards his family. Offering one's own parents in ransom is a conventional Arabic expression of extraordinary devotion.

translation: Glory to him who made lineages branch and spread.
The root unites them and the branch takes them apart.
13.sharh: A family tree shows kinship and distance at once. However far the tips of its branches spread, they still share a root.

translation: Some branches rise so high in human honour
that their growth takes the form of lofty palaces.
14.sharh: The image changes as the branches rise. Renown gives them the size and permanence of buildings visible from far away.

translation: Others have withered in reputation and distinction
through obscurity. May God bring them back to life.
15.sharh: Branches can also wither. Here what dies is the memory of a family's deeds, and the speaker hopes that memory can revive.

translation: Ancestry does not of itself confer pride on anyone,
nor does it defeat the ambitions of one who builds honour.
16.sharh: Descent gives no automatic claim to honour. The building image leaves room for someone to establish a reputation through their own effort.

translation: Many a nobleman has fallen from a towering summit
and tumbled down its slopes into the depths.
17.sharh: A high birth gives this man further to fall. The whole distance from summit to hollow measures how completely he can lose standing.

translation: Many a lowborn man's ambition has looked to the stars.
He climbs the high peaks to reach their summits.
18.sharh: The climber first lifts his eyes, then his feet. His ambition reverses the downward movement of the preceding verse.

translation: Ali, you stand above others in descent,
and among high deeds you dwell on the heights.
19.sharh: Ali possesses both inherited standing and distinction in his own right. His name echoes the Arabic words for rising and for the heights.

translation: Your father was the uncle of God's Messenger.
Mecca's valley floor witnessed his days there.
20.sharh: The genealogy begins one generation back. Mecca itself becomes a witness to Abu Talib's public protection of his nephew.

translation: He sheltered the Prophet from danger, defending him
with standing, sword and the verses he recited.
21.sharh: Abu Talib's social standing gave protection, and a poem spoken publicly could pledge that protection before the clan. Verse joins the sword in the list.

translation: He died without asking the Merciful for forgiveness.
Guidance has decrees that favour it.
22.sharh: The poet follows the Sunni account of Abu Talib's death. Shi'i tradition understands his public reserve as concealment of a faith he already held.

translation: Your illustrious grandfather was the Chosen One's grandfather too.
Quraysh knew the generous hand he extended.
23.sharh: The adjective magnifies the grandfather's stature. The “white hand” is an act of generosity remembered by the people who received it.

translation: When Quraysh reckons up its chiefs, is there anyone
like Shaybat al-Hamd to see it through a crisis?
24.sharh: The measure of a chief is what he can do when trouble comes. The name Shaybat al-Hamd draws the praise back to the grandfather just introduced.

translation: He renewed Zamzam, giving people its plentiful water,
and to this very day he gives it still.
25.sharh: In the Meccan account he recovered the well of Zamzam. Its continued flow allows the poet to speak of a man long dead as still giving drink.

translation: He went to Abraha to recover his she-camels
and entrusted the Kaaba to the Almighty to protect.
26.sharh: The Elephant story in the prophetic biography distinguishes the camels, for which their owner speaks, from the sanctuary, whose protection he leaves to God.

translation: His father was Amr of the heights, breaker of loaves,
slaughterer of lowing she-camels to feed his guests.
27.sharh: Hashim's name is traditionally linked to breaking bread for a meal. The sound of the camels gives another measure of what entertaining guests cost him.

translation: Among his customs he established the people's journey,
securing their summer travellers and their winter travellers alike.
28.sharh: The trade journeys tie the clan to places beyond Mecca. The choice of words recalls the compact of the winter and summer journeys in Quran 106.

translation: His descendants, the clan of the Prophet’s household, were barred
from taking alms from people’s wealth, to preserve their purity.
29.sharh: The legal rule about obligatory alms is used as a mark of the household's distinct standing. It is the receipt of alms that is at issue.

translation: His father, Abd Manaf, was a chief for whom
the tribe has kept a whole volume of its glories.
30.sharh: Another generation enters the family record. The imagined volume gives the tribe's accumulated memories the form of a book.

translation: He fathered those exceptional chiefs who concluded
their people's treaties for protection and ease.
31.sharh: The sons' alliances have practical consequences for Quraysh. Travellers gain protection, and the community can trade and live more easily.

translation: They are the kindred in the warning when it came down,
and God's Messenger stood among them to call them.
32.sharh: The command to warn one's closest kindred in Quran 26:214 brings this line of descent into the story of Muhammad's preaching.

translation: His father was Zayd, raised high by great ambitions.
He came from far away, making for the House.
33.sharh: Zayd is Qusayy. Traditions about his upbringing away from Mecca give the journey home a particular force in the genealogy.

translation: He drove out Khuza'a, and Mudar gained strength through him,
in a story its teller never tires of repeating.
34.sharh: Control of the sanctuary changes hands in the Meccan tradition. The verse also describes the people who keep telling the story.

translation: He held the standard and kept the House,
fed and watered pilgrims, and presided over the council.
35.sharh: Qusayy's authority consists of several offices. Carrying a standard, keeping a sanctuary and supplying pilgrims bring different responsibilities into one household.

translation: In his father Kilab the two parents
of our Prophet meet, sprung from fine-growing roots.
36.sharh: Muhammad's paternal and maternal lines meet at Kilab. The family tree, followed outwards a moment ago, is now traced back to a junction.

translation: He is Murra's son, descended in turn from Ka'b.
How many traces of Ka'b we can count.
37.sharh: The genealogy moves back two generations in a breath. Ka'b's surviving traces introduce a change from the list of names to an example.

translation: He established “to proceed” among the Arabs, and they followed,
composing that turn of speech on his model.
38.sharh: “To proceed” marks the turn from a speaker’s opening to the subject at hand. The poet gives Ka'b credit for the formula. Al-Subki records attributions to Quss ibn Sa'ida, Ka'b and David.

translation: His father Lu'ayy excelled his brothers.
That was a gift, and God its giver.
39.sharh: Lu'ayy stands out among men born into the same family. The poet treats the difference as an individual gift from God.

translation: Ghalib saw promise in him, and he proved
a generous chief like his forebears of honoured memory.
40.sharh: Ghalib is briefly a father watching a son grow. The son's later distinction fulfils the promise the father saw in him.

translation: Ghalib surpassed his peers and gained
a mastery plain to see among the sons of Fihr.
41.sharh: Ghalib's name suggests prevailing. His standing among the descendants of Fihr gives that sense a social setting.

translation: His father was Fihr, born to Malik, and he rose high.
Fihr’s grandfather al-Nadr laid the tribe’s foundations.
42.sharh: The poet looks past Fihr and Malik to al-Nadr. An ancestor now becomes the person who lays the foundations of a community.

translation: He embodies the tribe, for from his loins descended
Quraysh, rising to distinction and renown.
43.sharh: The poet locates Quraysh's common ancestry in al-Nadr. A competing genealogical reckoning places the boundary of Quraysh at Fihr.

translation: The line goes back to Kinana, its noble roots unbroken.
That is a great parent tribe, held high by the Arabs.
44.sharh: The Arabic word literally means a skull. Genealogists also use it for a major tribal stock from which other groups branch.

translation: On to Khuzayma, among Mudrika's sons,
from the loins of Ilyas, high in its upper reaches.
45.sharh: Each new name takes the listener another generation back. Height measures both distance from the present and the honour assigned to an ancestor.

translation: They are the chosen ones when Red Mudar
is praised. Whoever praises her recalls their glory.
46.sharh: The inherited name Red Mudar extends across the metrical break. Praising the larger tribal stock also honours the line the poet has been tracing.

translation: From Nizar onwards their story through the ages
is musk spreading its scent through every quarter.
47.sharh: A pedigree usually stretches through time. The scent of musk gives this reputation a way to travel through space as well.

translation: In the line of Ma'add son of Adnan their deeds
endure like an engraving. Who could erase them?
48.sharh: The scent of the previous line spreads, while engraving stays where it was made. The two images suggest different ways a name survives.

translation: They are of prophetic stock. Ishmael is their origin.
No one tells their eulogist to stop.
49.sharh: Ishmael stands at the far end of the traditional pedigree. The intervening names beyond Adnan are disputed, and the poem leaves that stretch unnamed.

translation: When groves thrive and the rain visits them early
in torrents, say how good their fruit is.
50.sharh: After looking backwards to ancestors, the poem looks forwards to children. A grove watered early prepares the image of a family's harvest.

translation: As for the salt flats and the refuse they hide,
their pastures are unwholesome even when they grow.
51.sharh: Salt ground supplies the counterexample to the fertile grove. Something can look like pasture yet fail those who feed there.

translation: Your field bore its fruit and flourished,
yielding leaders in every season.
52.sharh: The metaphor now acquires a human subject. In an echo of the Quranic tree that gives fruit in every season, the family continues to produce leaders.

translation: By God's command the Chaste One joined
the Prophet's line to a cord of her descendants.
53.sharh: Fatima carries the connection between the Prophet and her descendants. A cord replaces the tree and makes the maternal link visible.

translation: Your two sons are lords of the young lions in their final home.
Lordship seeks out those who deserve it.
54.sharh: The lion cubs are Hasan and Husayn. Their final destination evokes the tradition naming them leaders of the young men of Paradise.

translation: God's Prophet wrapped you all in his cloak,
and our mother lovingly relates it to the world.
55.sharh: The cloak gathers the four named family members into a single visible group. Aisha transmits a version of the scene, and Umm Salama figures in other versions.

translation: God bless Hasan, who so resembled the Chosen One,
and the wise course he offered when he rose to act.
56.sharh: Hasan's likeness to Muhammad introduces him. His own decision to make peace then gives the listener a distinct reason to remember him.

translation: An overflowing sea in knowledge and generosity,
a towering mountain when the dust storms rise.
57.sharh: The sea expresses abundance and the mountain steadiness. The praise needs both images because giving freely and holding firm are different virtues.

translation: A unifier, a chief, a leader wedded to generosity,
he gives away the caliphate as he gives away wealth.
58.sharh: Hasan's settlement with Mu'awiya gives generosity an unusually costly object. He parts with political authority to reunite two camps.

translation: He fulfilled a prophecy of God's Messenger,
reviving a practice of God's Messenger.
59.sharh: The allusion is to the prediction that God would reconcile two Muslim groups through Hasan. His act both fulfils the prediction and renews a prophetic practice.

translation: Husayn, the lion of the forest, bowed his head
to no one but his Creator.
60.sharh: The syntax holds Husayn's head in view before telling us whom he will bow to. Courage and worship meet in a single posture.

translation: Likened to the Commander of the Faithful, he went
to that same end, meeting it with the sword.
61.sharh: The Commander of the Faithful here is Husayn's father. The father's violent end foreshadows the son's, following the account of Hasan's settlement.

translation: With a handful of illustrious kin he faced the army
and met its horsemen, hurling his courage at them.
62.sharh: At Karbala the small company and the opposing cavalry are set against one another. Courage becomes the thing Husayn can throw back at them.

translation: Unjust spears reached him from all sides.
Woe to whoever ordered them, blessed whoever forbade them.
63.sharh: The poet asks the listener to look beyond the hands holding the spears. Giving or opposing an order carries moral weight of its own.

translation: He is the fortunate one, the most wretched his killer.
He is the martyr when the one who kneels comes to grief.
64.sharh: Death does not decide who has prospered. The contrast reaches beyond the battlefield to the humiliation of one brought to his knees.

translation: Your two daughters are Zaynab, with religion for her guide,
and Umm Kulthum, urged onward by faith.
65.sharh: Religion scouts the road for one daughter, while faith sings the other forward. The camel driver's image returns from the opening.

translation: A noble daughter bears her father's honour.
Only her equal can hope to marry her.
66.sharh: The verse states the poet's ideal of a match between families of comparable standing. It prepares the account of the daughters' marriages.

translation: Zaynab was won in marriage by a sea of generosity,
and Umm Kulthum by al-Faruq, who gained her hand.
67.sharh: The generous husband is Abd Allah ibn Ja'far. The poet accepts the reported marriage of Umm Kulthum to Umar. The Shi'i scholar al-Milani argues that, if the reports are accepted, they describe a contract made under pressure and give no proof of friendship between Ali and Umar.

translation: After Fatima you entered new bonds of kinship,
taking wives from tribes whose ties you honoured.
68.sharh: Marriage extends Ali's relationships beyond the immediate family. Each new wife brings a tie to another tribal community.

translation: You fathered children whose support went to the right.
Their names undo the claim and disprove it.
69.sharh: The ensuing names, some shared with the early caliphs, carry a polemical argument for the poet. A shared name alone cannot establish a father's private motive.

translation: Muhammad, Abu Bakr, Ja'far and
Abbas. How noble the children and the man who named them.
70.sharh: The roll call is part of the argument about names. The Arabic article of al-Abbas falls in the first half, and the name itself opens the second.

translation: Yahya, bold Uthman, and Umar too.
Fine are these loyal kin. Give them your loyalty.
71.sharh: The list ends in an appeal to the listener. The word for these close kin carries the sense of people who incline towards one another.

translation: Remember Ubayd and Abd Allah and weep for them.
Their blood flowed, and the sword set it flowing.
72.sharh: The roll call becomes a lament. Genealogical reports differ over the identification and deaths of sons with these names.

translation: Most of them indeed met their end by the sword.
So a free man feels its fire and makes others feel it.
73.sharh: Two closely related verbs give the closing line its movement. The free man endures the fire of battle and can bring others into it.

translation: Ahmad raised you in his own household. How fine,
how fine an upbringing commended by revelation.
74.sharh: Ahmad is Muhammad. A doubled expression of admiration straddles the pause, drawing attention to the household in which Ali grew up.

translation: You were the close companion of God's Messenger, following
his bearing in the traits you showed.
75.sharh: The saddlecloth in the Arabic image hardly leaves its place. Constant companionship makes Muhammad's bearing recognisable in Ali's behaviour.

translation: You witnessed his circumstances in every struggle,
a happiness that brought delight or a hardship he endured.
76.sharh: Ali sees events at close quarters. Joy as well as adversity establishes the range of his experience of Muhammad's life.

translation: You answered when he called you to
the good of your life here and the life that follows.
77.sharh: The call and the response share the first line. Its promise spans the whole of a life and what follows it.

translation: Though young, you were among the earliest to embrace Islam,
with the three, the Merciful their guide.
78.sharh: The “three” evoke the company of the first believers. Accounts distinguish categories such as first woman, adult man or boy, and give different orders.

translation: You were the first to pray, once prayer was enjoined,
beside the Prophet, performing it in fear.
79.sharh: Early belief takes visible form in a shared act of worship. Fear recalls the insecurity of the first believers in Mecca.

translation: On the day he emigrated, he entrusted his charge to you,
and you lay in the Chosen One's bed as a decoy.
80.sharh: The traditional migration account gives Ali both a trust to discharge and a bed to occupy. His presence conceals Muhammad's departure.

translation: You hurried after him to reunite the household,
guarding and protecting the Fatimas on the way.
81.sharh: The reunion follows the separation of the migration. “The Fatimas” is a collective for women bearing that name, whose identification varies in the reports.

translation: God chose you as husband for the Chaste One.
Say that the radiant part of him has found her match.
82.sharh: Fatima is called a part of the Prophet in a well-known saying. The marriage joins Ali to a woman whose relationship to her father is expressed in bodily terms.

translation: You lived beside the Messenger's dwellings.
How much wisdom and guidance you took from his light.
83.sharh: A neighbour can carry a flame home from a nearby light. The same closeness allows instruction to pass from one household to the other.

translation: You hung back from no expedition and no danger,
bearer of banners you raised in victory,
84.sharh: The banners take the listener from home to the expeditions. The sweeping first line runs straight into the express exception in the next verse.

translation: except at Tabuk. You remained in Taba,
at Ahmad's command, in charge there.
85.sharh: The exception is an assignment in Medina while the expedition goes to Tabuk. Taba is the poet's form of a traditional name of Medina.

translation: You stood to him as Aaron stood in kinship
to the one God spoke to. That likeness is enough for me.
86.sharh: The one God spoke to is Moses. The Tabuk tradition compares Ali to Aaron in relation to his brother and expressly reserves prophethood.

translation: God sent down verses by which past treaties
with the unbelievers were renounced.
87.sharh: The opening of Quran 9 concerns treaty obligations. Its proclamation distinguishes groups whose terms lapse from those whose agreements must run their course.

translation: You received the verses from God's Messenger and carried them,
urging his riding camel al-Adba onwards.
88.sharh: The named mount makes delivery of the proclamation a physical journey. The messenger carries words entrusted to him and rides the Prophet's own camel.

translation: At last you took the message to the assembled pilgrims,
casting its words upon their ears like stones.
89.sharh: The hardness of stone gives weight to a spoken announcement. The assembly has to hear terms that change its former arrangements.

translation: “Disavowal.” The echo goes on and on,
and the universe listens in submission to its message.
90.sharh: “Disavowal” is the sura's opening word. The imagined echo carries a public announcement far beyond its first audience.

translation: At the pool the Chosen One clothed you in honour,
with kin to whom the Lord enjoined devotion.
91.sharh: At Ghadir Khumm a prophetic declaration singles Ali out. Sunni and Shi'i traditions understand the authority conveyed there differently, a distinction central to this passage.

translation: On the day the world darkened, when the lights went out
that had shone on Medina from its guide’s lamp niche,
92.sharh: A lamp niche holds and concentrates light. Its extinction figures Muhammad's death and prepares the sound of mourning that follows.

translation: sobbing rose from his bewildered Companions
like a droning sound that filled Medina on every side.
93.sharh: The city has lost its light and gained another sound. The continuous hum conveys many individual voices grieving together.

translation: You washed God's Messenger, and in the washing
your hands grew clean. May God reward them with Paradise.
94.sharh: Ali washes the Prophet's body for burial. The grammar turns the washing back upon the hands that perform it, as though service itself purified them.

translation: You went down into his grave, carrying him to the burial niche,
bidding farewell in tears to a companionship you mourn.
95.sharh: The niche is the recess where the body is laid. A lifetime of proximity ends in the intimate act of lowering a companion into his grave.

translation: On the day of Badr, by God, there set out
a company of the best people on earth.
96.sharh: Badr opens the military recollections. The oath marks the poet's estimate of the people in that small company before he describes anything they did.

translation: There you travelled with God's Messenger, taking turns
on the camel that covered the distance to each goal.
97.sharh: To share a camel was to take one's turn walking too. The recollection brings the grand description of the company down to the road beneath their feet.

translation: You carried his white standard with assurance
among young men of Quraysh whom no one could rival.
98.sharh: The colour makes the standard visible above the young men. Ali's place within the company is marked by what he is trusted to carry.

translation: Had faith not been kept with Abd al-Dar, no one
but you would have borne the standard when the summons came.
99.sharh: Abd al-Dar stands for a clan traditionally entrusted with the standard. Keeping faith with it explains, in the poet's account, why another man could bear it.

translation: Sakhina advanced with its champions,
intent on unbelief and on barring the way to Islam.
100.sharh: The hostile nickname marks the Meccan side at Badr. Men of Quraysh appear on both sides of the encounter.

translation: They called for single combat. You answered the call like
a lion, cleaving them with a bright blade in your right hand.
101.sharh: A fixed challenge to come down and fight is answered by a deed. The “white one” in Ali's hand is a polished sword.

translation: “These two are adversaries” came down about you that day.
Each reader brings its events to life again.
102.sharh: A report associates Quran 22:19 with the opposing champions at Badr. The present-tense reader gives the remembered event a new hearing.

translation: And when the confederates advanced in numbers,
with God to forsake them and God to put them to shame,
103.sharh: The confederate attack on Medina is a new episode. The poet tells the listener the campaign's outcome before introducing its individual challenger.

translation: Amr ibn Wudd forced his way across the dug trench, chanting rajaz,
urging on a short-coated mare.
104.sharh: The collective army gives way to a mounted individual. His short rhythmic chant makes an audible challenge before the encounter with Ali.

translation: Armed to the teeth, he spread fear among the Arabs,
among those who lived in towns and those in the desert.
105.sharh: The opponent's reputation travels farther than his horse. Town and desert together measure the reach of the name Ali has to face.

translation: You advanced to check him, striking him with your sword,
and he fell in the depths of its valley.
106.sharh: The repeated consonants in the Arabic link checking the charge to striking the rider. His fall completes the motion that began with the leap across the trench.

translation: Remember Khaybar, whose strongholds towered beyond a raid's reach
and whose fortresses held out.
107.sharh: The episode begins with height and inaccessibility. Two words for strongholds set the scale of the obstacle before Ali is called forward.

translation: The Jews there thought the stronghold would protect them
and its wall suffice them for all time.
108.sharh: The line attributes confidence in a particular fortress to Khaybar's Jewish defenders. Its promised permanence sets up the reversal to come.

translation: The Messenger said, “I shall give my standard to a man
whose sign is love. He will bring it victory.”
109.sharh: The underlying report gives love a reciprocal sense. The bearer loves God and his Messenger and is loved by them, and victory is promised through him.

translation: “Call Ali.” They said, “He has been suffering
since yesterday with an inflammation that hurts his eye.”
110.sharh: The urgent call meets an unexpected answer about an inflamed eye. The bodily weakness makes the choice of standard-bearer appear all the more surprising.

translation: He came supported, his eye dim with soreness.
The Chosen One spits on it, and God heals it.
111.sharh: Ali has to be helped forward. In the Khaybar tradition Muhammad applies his saliva to the sore eyes and Ali recovers.

translation: “Proceed gently, Ali. Our aim
is to guide people, far and near.”
112.sharh: The charge to the standard-bearer includes an instruction to take his time. In the underlying report the people are to be invited to Islam first.

translation: At Hunayn the people’s very numbers did them harm.
The fierce onslaught taught them that.
113.sharh: The line recalls Quran 9:25 on confidence in numbers at Hunayn. The attack itself delivers the lesson.

translation: The army faltered and fear came over everyone,
each turning in terror in a different direction.
114.sharh: The crowd that took pride in its number breaks into separate individuals. Each now has a direction of his own.

translation: Except the Messenger and Companions with a long record
of early service, who stood firm against its fury.
115.sharh: “A foot” can mean prior standing or a record of service. Their past commitment is made visible in the fact that they remain on the field.

translation: A little band fought devotedly in front of its leader,
offering him their lives in love, as he offers his for them.
116.sharh: The second half turns its own syntax around. The little band's willingness to give their lives is answered by the leader's concern for theirs.

translation: You were among them, busy in death's marketplace,
measuring out heads with your sword, giving full measure.
117.sharh: The marketplace language is deliberately unsettling. A trader measures goods and makes up the full amount, while here the sword does the reckoning.

translation: There you hamstrung a tame mount whose rider
kept assailing the ranks and devastating them.
118.sharh: The focus narrows to the mount supporting a persistent attacker. Its fall provides the narrative hinge between the panic and the recovery.

translation: The fierce assault was checked, and a cloud cleared
whose flashing light had snatched away men's sight.
119.sharh: A cloud's exposed flash evokes the blinding confusion of the assault. As it passes, the people on the field can see again.

translation: God gave mastery over Nasr and Jusham
and over Thaqif when they were led by their forelocks.
120.sharh: The names specify tribal opponents, and the forelock is an image of subjection. The close compresses a campaign whose aftermath continued beyond the battle.

translation: After the backbreaking blow that came close
to effacing the faith through its terrible consequences,
121.sharh: Muhammad's death was first a personal bereavement. The poem now returns to it as a crisis in the public life of the community.

translation: God came to the rescue through al-Siddiq in a time of trial
on the day of the portico, and its darkness cleared.
122.sharh: The portico is the meeting place where Abu Bakr received allegiance. The poet presents the decision as providential relief in a dark hour.

translation: It was a sudden decision that took precedence once occasion arose
for a pledge the Helpers had intended.
123.sharh: The word for a sudden decision echoes Umar's later description of the pledge. The Helpers of Medina had already gathered to discuss leadership.

translation: You gave your pledge the day after the first pledge,
alongside al-Zubayr. We relate this from al-Khudri.
124.sharh: Abu al-Faraj names Abu Sa'id al-Khudri as his source for an early pledge. In Aisha's account in Bukhari, Ali pledges after Fatima dies, six months after Muhammad. Some scholars reconcile the two reports by distinguishing a first pledge from a renewal.

translation: You did not begrudge al-Siddiq his gift,
act on your own authority or covet it yourself.
125.sharh: The poet clears Ali of three motives for disagreement. The following verse supplies a distinct complaint he considers legitimate.

translation: What grieved you was to have no say in their deliberations,
when you had sought their counsel and given them yours.
126.sharh: The poet places Ali’s grievance in being left out of the decision. The exchange of advice in the second half recalls the voice he had expected to have.

translation: And after the Messenger's daughter joined him
in the eternal garden, when her death was announced,
127.sharh: Fatima's death marks a change in the account of the relationship between Ali and Abu Bakr. The sentence waits for their meeting in the next verse.

translation: you made peace when al-Siddiq came to you, and out burst
a spring of affection, flooding its channels.
128.sharh: A spring breaking out makes reconciliation visible. In the poet's reading, the course of the water was there even while affection was obstructed.

translation: You accompanied him as an adviser in his undertakings.
He carried matters of government through with your counsel.
129.sharh: Counsel gives the restored relationship a practical form. The poem assigns Ali a role in decisions taken during Abu Bakr's rule.

translation: Afterwards you lived in accord with al-Faruq,
serving the community as its judge with even scales.
130.sharh: Al-Faruq is Umar. An even balance makes the virtue expected of a judge concrete in the account of their association.

translation: You continued to acknowledge a place for the two elders
below the Messenger, one no living man could approach.
131.sharh: The “two elders” are Abu Bakr and Umar. The poet attributes to Ali the order of merit familiar from Sunni tradition.

translation: Many a man you rebuked for preferring you,
chastising him with the whip to deter such folly.
132.sharh: Reports differ in form, some describing a threat of punishment. The poet stages the censure as a punishment carried out.

translation: You pledged allegiance to Uthman of the Two Lights, approving
a consultation whose aims were surrounded by guidance.
133.sharh: Uthman emerged from the council appointed by Umar. The epithet recalls his marriages, in succession, to two daughters of Muhammad.

translation: You were the first to give him your pledge,
and the grandson the last in the house to defend him.
134.sharh: The grandson is Hasan. “First” and “last” link the father's allegiance to the son's defence of Uthman, whose final siege is reported in differing detail.

translation: You are their fourth in rule and rank,
degrees of honour built upon devotion.
135.sharh: Ali was historically fourth in succession. Ranking him fourth in merit expresses the Sunni evaluation adopted by the poet.

translation: Each of you takes from God's Messenger
a full moon that shines when the night grows black.
136.sharh: Each caliph borrows light from Muhammad's example. The darker the public crisis, the more visible that inherited light becomes.

translation: The caliphs are Islam's fortress,
a shield for the sacred law against whoever shoots at it.
137.sharh: The fortress shelters a community. The shield takes an approaching missile on its behalf, extending the first image into a second.

translation: Those guided rulers lead followers free of misery
towards deliverance, however long its waterless wastes.
138.sharh: The rightly guided rulers become guides in turn. Waterless stretches convey the hardship and length of the journey towards salvation.

translation: They make revealed texts their guide
and know them so well their meanings are clear.
139.sharh: Their authority is itself guided. Following revelation also requires the knowledge to interpret what it says.

translation: They hasten to good deeds as in a race
and mount up whenever the caller summons them.
140.sharh: Racing and mounting for a summons both convey readiness. The praised quality is how quickly a call turns into action.

translation: They bring plenty when people's hands are barren
and turn away from the world and all it holds.
141.sharh: Other hands are imagined as land in drought. These men can restore plenty because the things they give are things they do not cling to.

translation: Kin by marriage to Ahmad, they won the honour of aiding him,
wholly free of self-serving desires.
142.sharh: All four are connected to Muhammad by marriage. The poet's judgement on their motives prepares his treatment of conflicts that followed.

translation: In the heady days of conquest the horizons smiled,
time itself rejoiced and its days were glad.
143.sharh: The opening is deliberately bright. Even time seems to share the elation of success, making the darkening that follows more abrupt.

translation: Clarity turned murky as its springs ran low.
The green plants withered and the winds scattered them.
144.sharh: Political disorder is experienced as a landscape losing water. The wind then carries off what the soil can no longer sustain.

translation: Delegations had alighted in the month of pilgrimage
around Mecca, hoping for their Maker's favour.
145.sharh: The pilgrims gathering around Mecca supply a simultaneous scene. Uthman's siege in the next verse takes place in Medina.

translation: A sweeping sedition rose treacherously against the elder.
May God withhold his blessing from whoever fanned it.
146.sharh: The elder is Uthman. The vocabulary of fire changes the question from who was present to who kept the revolt burning.

translation: Brutes from the frontier came in a clamorous host,
like snakes crawling to a hole.
147.sharh: The invective belongs to the poet's portrait of the besiegers. The snake image turns the arrival of a noisy force into a movement of menace.

translation: They encircled the house, respecting neither its owner's early service
nor the privacy of those within.
148.sharh: A public conflict reaches the domestic threshold. The owner's past service and the privacy of the household are two distinct claims on the attackers.

translation: They forged letters in your name which you never wrote,
their scribe wielding the pen while the Devil dictated.
149.sharh: The siege narratives include competing accounts of letters and their authorship. The poet accepts forgery and imagines the Devil dictating the words.

translation: You neither wrote nor ordered them, and your cause
did not coincide with a faction whose claims failed.
150.sharh: The poet distinguishes writing a message, commissioning it and sharing its purpose. He clears Ali on each count.

translation: Alas for them. They brought down a mountain in their midst
that had held their land firm against its swaying.
151.sharh: The mountain steadies the very ground of the men who pull it down. The image turns their blow against their own community.

translation: Remember Hudhayfa's account of a door that held trials back.
Once broken, they spread far and wide.
152.sharh: Hudhayfa's famous report identifies the door as Umar. Its appearance in the account of Uthman's murder links successive crises without changing the door's original identity.

translation: The mill of evil turned. The days stood silent,
bereaved, longing for their former joys.
153.sharh: A mill moves relentlessly while the bereaved can only stand still. The days themselves seem to mourn for the happiness with which the previous section opened.

translation: Medina became hostage to a handful of men,
and the people's lords were lorded over by their clients.
154.sharh: The same Arabic root names the lords and the act of ruling them. The grammatical reversal embodies the poet's picture of authority turned upside down.

translation: People's eyes looked to you in longing.
Like a star in the black of night, you guided them.
155.sharh: The people look up together as travellers do when seeking a star. The comparison presents Ali as a point by which they can find their bearings.

translation: They pledged to you upon the ruins of a realm,
and there among them you began to rebuild it on the ruins.
156.sharh: Rubble appears in both halves. The same place in which allegiance is given is the site where governing has to begin.

translation: You thought affairs should settle down in peace
until the judge could exercise his authority.
157.sharh: The poet makes a functioning court a condition for punishment. That sequencing of political order and legal redress frames the coming disagreement.

translation: You meant to disperse the rabble who had assembled,
moving them out of Medina to the provincial towns.
158.sharh: Concentrated force in Medina is the difficulty the speaker identifies. The provincial garrison towns provide the other end of the proposed movement.

translation: In all you attempted you exercised your judgement.
God sets his wisdom at work in what he decrees.
159.sharh: A ruler has to form a judgement under pressure. The poet leaves the outcome within a divine order that the human decision-maker cannot command.

translation: Groups opposed you, seeking swift retribution
against the offenders, a claim they would not defer.
160.sharh: The poet gives the opposition a specific legal demand and stresses its urgency. Accounts of the political opposition also describe wider disagreements.

translation: Among them was al-Zubayr, the Messenger's devoted helper.
His deeds rank among the most prized in Islam.
161.sharh: The first opponent named retains a title of honour. That choice matters to a poem seeking to speak well of Companions on both sides.

translation: And Talha ibn Ubayd Allah, whose right hand was crippled
shielding the Prophet, willing to give himself for him.
162.sharh: Talha's injured hand recalls Uhud. It gives his earlier protection of Muhammad a bodily trace that survives into the civil-war narrative.

translation: And our mother, the Guide’s pearl and his delight.
How gracious and noble she is. Ruin to whoever hates her.
163.sharh: “Our mother” identifies Aisha through the Quranic designation for the Prophet's wives. Her place in his household shapes how the poet asks the audience to regard her.

translation: She went with the army in a screened litter on a camel.
You went with the troops to turn them back.
164.sharh: The opposing movements put the camel at the centre before the fighting begins. The battle near Basra took its familiar name from Aisha's mount.

translation: That day you all made the same claim for justice.
Your differences lay in the paths that led to it.
165.sharh: The poet reconciles the parties by assigning them one end and different means. Historians also describe disagreements over political authority itself.

translation: On the day you met, messengers sprang up between you,
hurrying there and back to mend the breach.
166.sharh: The envoys cross the very space the armies may fight over. Their going and returning turns an attempt at settlement into a visible pattern.

translation: You passed the night on good terms, old grudges folded away.
Someone else spent it feeding the flames.
167.sharh: A single night contains reconciliation and the undoing of it. This is one transmitted explanation of how the Battle of the Camel began.

translation: Without intrigues the dust would never have risen,
nor lives ebbed away once the keen swords came out.
168.sharh: The poet makes intrigue decisive. The sources disagree about how close the parties came to peace and about who set the fighting in motion.

translation: You stood giving orders in the arena of champions
while the mother of dust swept through its quarters.
169.sharh: “Mother of dust” personifies the turmoil of battle. Against that moving backdrop Ali is held still for the words he addresses to the fighters.

translation: “Come back to your senses. Sheathe your swords.
Stay your hands.” You spoke with resolve.
170.sharh: The same Arabic verb can describe drawing a sword or sheathing it. The command to stay their hands makes the intended sense here clear.

translation: War resembles sparks of fire. Once kindled,
it becomes a blaze that scorches everyone.
171.sharh: A spark is small enough for one person to start. The fire it becomes is beyond either side's ability to reserve for its opponent.

translation: A wretch struck al-Zubayr dead and rolled his head away,
a crime that earned its perpetrator woe.
172.sharh: Al-Zubayr is remembered as having left the battlefield before his death. The poet assigns dishonour to the killer and laments the victim.

translation: Talha fell to a taut-drawn bow.
What a shot, bringing ruin upon the archer.
173.sharh: The arrow kills Talha, while the moral consequence falls on its archer. A strand of the historical tradition names Marwan, whom the verse leaves unnamed.

translation: Dust covered the sunlight till it went out,
and our mother stood between her assailants and defenders.
174.sharh: The camel is a focus both for attack and for protection. The darkened daylight makes Aisha's vulnerability in the middle of the fighting more vivid.

translation: Seventy champions lost their lives
at the halter, and the mother's eye wept for them.
175.sharh: Holding the halter meant staying at the centre of the battle. Seventy is the poem's count, while accounts of the losses around the camel vary.

translation: When the dust cleared you finished off no fallen man.
Instead you turned to tend the wounded.
176.sharh: The clearing air marks a change in obligation towards the fallen. The defeated are presented as wounded people entitled to care.

translation: You took no captives and claimed none of their belongings as spoils.
You gave no one leave to enslave the women.
177.sharh: The treatment of defeated Muslims became an important precedent in legal discussions of rebellion. The poet brings out its consequences for property and for women.

translation: That is a soul held safe by religion's bridle
when the tempter's prompting lures other souls away.
178.sharh: The bridle is turned inward. What must be controlled after victory is the victor's own desire.

translation: In Syria a party broke away from you.
It withheld its pledge and carried out its governor's orders.
179.sharh: The scene shifts from Basra to Syria. Withholding allegiance leaves the governor's authority set against that claimed by the new caliph.

translation: They called for vengeance for Uthman, demanding
that trusts be restored to their rightful owners.
180.sharh: Language echoing Quran 4:58 casts retribution as a trust owed to the victim's kin. It is the claim made by the Syrian side in this account.

translation: They thought the wrong immense and feared
lest blood go unavenged, its shedder lost from sight.
181.sharh: To “lose” blood in this idiom is to let a killing go without redress. Failure to identify the person responsible gives the concern its force.

translation: At their head was the scribe of revelation, for whom
eminent men testified to trustworthiness and distinction.
182.sharh: Mu'awiya is introduced through the Sunni tradition that remembers him as a scribe for Muhammad. The honorific sets the terms in which this poet discusses Ali's opponent.

translation: A man of Abd Shams, whose knee-band no rashness loosened
when other men's bands flew loose with them.
183.sharh: A seated man could bind his knees up with a cloth. Keeping it in place while others spring up in agitation conveys the composure attributed to Mu'awiya.

translation: You advanced resolutely with the army to bend them
back to obedience, hoping for the offender's return.
184.sharh: Bending someone back and hoping they will return express different aspects of Ali's purpose. Restoring allegiance is still the poem's stated object.

translation: You encamped with your soldiers at Siffin and waited,
your kinsman leading troops a match for yours.
185.sharh: The “cousin” is a more distant kinsman in Quraysh. The matching armies foreshadow a costly struggle that neither side settles quickly.

translation: When the sacred month slipped away, a runner
went among the battalions to rouse them.
186.sharh: The month's passing changes the rhythm of the narrative. The first movement we see is someone carrying an appeal from unit to unit.

translation: Horsemen met horsemen equal in number,
and troops met troops that could match them.
187.sharh: The two halves mirror each army back to itself. The balance of wording makes the claimed balance of forces audible.

translation: People fought for religion and conviction,
as one who knows the gardens of Paradise and seeks them.
188.sharh: The poet gives conviction to people on both sides. Paradise is what each believes he is seeking, an explanation of motive supplied by the poem.

translation: No young man fled his equal in panic,
no standard fell from its bearer's hand.
189.sharh: Personal combat and the collective standard each supply a test of steadiness. Both sides hold their ground in this picture.

translation: Blood flowed and lives turned in the mill.
Blood is war's fuel and kindles it.
190.sharh: The mill consumes lives and the fire feeds on blood. Each death supplies another reason for the fighting to continue.

translation: If a division flags, killing rouses it.
If a front dies down, killing sets it alight.
191.sharh: The previous metaphor becomes a cycle in the ranks. A lull on either side is broken by the killing that has already taken place.

translation: War went back and forth through bloodstained days.
Its blaze nearly consumed the Arabs.
192.sharh: Advantage passes between the two sides while losses accumulate. Calling the days bloodstained makes the duration of the fighting part of its toll.

translation: What their spearheads spill dyes the earth.
In pity the earth's eyes well over.
193.sharh: The earth receives blood and seems to answer with tears. Its surface becomes a face capable of pity for the people fighting upon it.

translation: At last Ammar fell, and the state of the rightly guided
became distinct from that of the transgressing party.
194.sharh: A prophetic report says a transgressing party would kill Ammar. His death while fighting for Ali becomes the poet's criterion for judging the two sides.

translation: By dying he gave life to his companions, who rose up.
His death broke his opponents and brought them to their knees.
195.sharh: Ammar's death has opposite effects in the two armies. The paradox of a dead man giving life expresses the recovery of his companions' resolve.

translation: The Syrian host took refuge on the hill, their resolve broken
though the pursuit of justice had spurred them on.
196.sharh: The Syrians take refuge on the hill after Ammar’s death. The poet pictures the pursuit of justice as the camel-driver who had urged them on, and still credits them with that motive as their courage fails.

translation: They called for judgement by God's verses. The soldiers raised
copies of the Quran high on their spears.
197.sharh: Spears acquire a second function as supports for copies or leaves of the Quran. Accounts differ about the calculations behind the appeal.

translation: You stopped before the Book of God, consenting
in reverence and worship to the Sovereign's judgement.
198.sharh: The poet foregrounds Ali's reverence for scripture. Historical accounts also record strong pressure from within his own army to accept arbitration.

translation: Abu Musa negotiated on your behalf,
a teacher of the Recitation, of its reading and understanding.
199.sharh: Abu Musa's reputation as a Quran teacher suits the appeal to scripture. Accounts of his appointment describe disagreement within Ali's camp.

translation: Amr represented the Syrians, and the two agreed
to seek consultation, anxious to pursue it.
200.sharh: The poem gives the negotiations a common aim. The terms and outcome of the arbitration are contested, and this closing couplet offers no transcript of an agreement.

translation: Judgement belongs to God. People are entrusted
with his laws and carry them out as best they can.
201.sharh: Muslim records the seceders' cry, “Judgement belongs to God alone.” Abu al-Faraj echoes it and adds that people bear responsibility for applying divine law.

translation: Happiest in station in both worlds
is one who makes his soul a servant of its Creator.
202.sharh: The first subject of discipline here is one's own self. That choice prepares the criticism of imposing severity on other people.

translation: Harshest are those who go to extremes, sacrificing
God’s law for a severity at odds with it.
203.sharh: In the recited wording, excessive strictness comes at the cost of divine law itself. The studio card says the law was replaced. Both readings explain why the next half calls this severity an enemy of the law.

translation: Most ignorant of the Quran are those who recite it
and its verses go no further than their collarbones.
204.sharh: A prophetic description of recitation going no farther than the throat underlies the image. The listener hears words that, in the poet's judgement, have not shaped the speaker's understanding.

translation: Most foolish in all the land is a youth
who vies with elders taught by God's Messenger.
205.sharh: A young man's claim to rival older Companions is measured against their direct experience of Muhammad's teaching.

translation: No sooner had you returned from arbitration than
dogs in your army barked in imitation of their howler.
206.sharh: The barking is the poet's abusive comparison for dissent spreading through the ranks. It also introduces the leader whose voice the group is said to echo.

translation: Al-Rasibi, their ill-guiding leader, kept vigil
through the hours of the night, remembering God.
207.sharh: Al-Rasibi's night-long devotion is conceded even in a hostile portrait. For the poet, intense worship and sound judgement can come apart.

translation: They declared you an unbeliever. Say, by God, it has grown so lean
that no buyer could be hoped for even at a copper coin.
208.sharh: Their accusation is pictured as an emaciated animal or worthless merchandise. Even the smallest coin would fail to find it a buyer.

translation: A band of rough men keeps
distorting the verses through ignorance, twisting them awry.
209.sharh: Twisting is a physical image for forcing a verse into a meaning. The charge concerns how the group reads and applies scripture.

translation: They take verses revealed about unbelievers
and apply them to the Companions, pressing on astonishingly far.
210.sharh: The fault is a change of referent. A judgement originally directed at unbelievers is transferred to fellow Muslims.

translation: You stood among them to guide them by revelation's light,
debating them with proofs born of understanding.
211.sharh: Ali first appears as an interpreter addressing people who still share his scripture. Evidence and the understanding of its setting belong together.

translation: Ibn Abbas stood among them and silenced their objections.
He brought a third back from their misleader's views.
212.sharh: Ibn Abbas persuades some of the seceders to return. The third in the verse fits the account in al-Nasa'i, where two thousand return out of six thousand. Other accounts give different totals.

translation: You did not begin by shunning them or fighting them.
You called them transgressors and left their guidance to God.
213.sharh: Calling them a transgressing party still leaves room for their return. The poet distinguishes that judgement from the decision to fight.

translation: You denied them neither public revenue nor assistance,
nor barred those who came to God's houses.
214.sharh: The often-reported policy concerns both a share in public revenues and access to mosques. The disagreement did not by itself cancel either.

translation: But they persisted blindly in error and dared
to spill blood whose crimson betrayed the wrong.
215.sharh: The line marks a change from argument to violent acts attributed to the seceders. The blood's colour seems to testify against those who shed it.

translation: You roused your army with traditions, urging them
to battle. You traced those sayings to the Prophet, whom God kept from error.
216.sharh: Ali invokes sayings about the seceders. By calling Muhammad divinely protected from error, the poet conveys the authority Ali claims for the words he passes on.

translation: When the two forces at last came face to face,
the wretched one stood to instruct his rough followers.
217.sharh: The promised speech is framed by the poet's verdict on its speaker. It represents the seceders' commander at close quarters before the clash.

translation: “Cast down the spears. Draw the sword and do not falter.
The everlasting garden is sweet to whoever seeks it.”
218.sharh: These are words the poem puts in the opposing commander's mouth. The promise of Paradise explains his men's resolve within the scene.

translation: So in their folly they flung away their Khatt spears.
Folly wears out everyone who tries to cure it.
219.sharh: An old proverbial line about folly answers the commander's speech. The poet treats the discarded spears as the visible consequence of a misjudgement.

translation: You pierced them with the army's spears, reaping them
like ears of grain bent towards the harvester.
220.sharh: The spears discarded in the preceding verse are answered by the other army's spears. Bending grain gives the deaths an image of terrible ease.

translation: Man of Murad, may God curse you for a traitor.
What a wretched offering you make to God.
221.sharh: The addressee changes to Ali's assassin. The bitter irony lies in calling a murder an offering meant to bring its giver close to God.

translation: You stained his beard with blood from a head once filled
with justice for the people and instruction for reciters.
222.sharh: Blood acts as dye for the beard. The head that received the wound is remembered for what the community received from its learning.

translation: Yours was no bravery. You came from behind,
like a viper treacherously striking whoever turns his back.
223.sharh: The snake image is an accusation of treachery. The narrative details of the attack vary, while the poet fixes attention on the victim's vulnerability.

translation: When seventeen nights of the fasting month had passed,
you made hearts bleed by striking their shepherd's head.
224.sharh: The poet dates the blow to 17 Ramadan. Other accounts place it on the nineteenth. The shepherd's bodily wound becomes a wound shared by his people.

translation: A blow from a wretch who wanted nothing by it
except to efface the face of faith and disfigure it.
225.sharh: An old verse attributed to Imran ibn Hittan praised a blow by a “pious man”. Replacing that word with “wretch” reverses the force of the borrowed opening.

translation: Ali lived on in patient endurance
for two days, his spirit yearning for its Maker.
226.sharh: The two days belong to the chronology chosen by the poem. The focus passes from the wounded body to the direction of Ali's longing.

translation: His soul flowed out pure towards eternity
to join the company in the highest part of Paradise.
227.sharh: The departure is gentle after the violence of the wound. Joining a travelling company becomes an image of reunion in Paradise.

translation: With his death and the few months that followed
under the pledge to Hasan, its much-praised ruler,
228.sharh: Hasan's brief tenure is counted along with his father's. The grammatical conclusion waits until the next verse.

translation: a rightly guided caliphate came to its close. A company passed away
whose endeavours had followed the Chosen One's footsteps.
229.sharh: Counting Hasan's months is a Sunni interpretation of the tradition assigning thirty years to the caliphate. Footsteps unite the successive rulers in the poet's account.

translation: Recognise them as men of distinction, remember their story,
follow their traces and shun whoever opposes them.
230.sharh: Four imperatives turn history into a demand on the listener. Remembering the rulers is the beginning of emulating their conduct.

translation: Follower of the radiant Sunna, you champion it
with a life that shows it plainly to the world.
231.sharh: The conclusion addresses Ali as a follower of Muhammad's example. His own life is presented as a way of making that example legible.

translation: Subduer of blameworthy innovations, you defeat them
with the spear of truth, striking them down.
232.sharh: The weapon now belongs to an argument. Practices the poet condemns are personified as opponents struck by truth.

translation: You honoured the Sunna of the best of creation with all your effort.
Your constant care was to follow its example.
233.sharh: Habit and deliberate care reinforce each other. Prayer and pilgrimage will supply concrete examples of what following the Sunna meant here.

translation: Imran said, “This man has called to our minds
Ahmad's prayer as we used to perform it.”
234.sharh: Imran ibn Husayn recalled the Prophet's prayer when he saw Ali lead worship. The report mentions the way Ali marked the movements with the takbir.

translation: You differed openly with Uthman of the Two Lights
over combining the pilgrimage rites, declaring your intent aloud.
235.sharh: The dispute concerns how the lesser and greater pilgrimages may be performed together. Ali makes his position audible in the pilgrim's ritual invocation.

translation: You spoke a word to him that became a saying
for a community following in its forebears' steps.
236.sharh: Before giving the words themselves, the poet imagines their later audience. A statement in a particular disagreement becomes a maxim about precedent.

translation: “No, Uthman, I will not leave his practice
for a saying of men, whoever utters it.”
237.sharh: This paraphrases Ali's reported reply in the pilgrimage dispute. The general “whoever” extends the principle beyond the immediate disagreement.

translation: You were the one who burned the extremists when they disbelieved
and made a god of you alongside the Merciful.
238.sharh: Bukhari reports the burning and Ibn Abbas's objection to the method. The identification of those punished as people who deified Ali belongs to a particular account.

translation: You never claimed infallibility for the Prophet's family.
Indeed we relate from you explicit words against it.
239.sharh: The poet argues against a doctrine of infallibility. Twelver Shi'i teaching understands the infallibility of the imams differently, so this is an argument within a historical disagreement.

translation: You said, “We were given no exclusive knowledge,
save insights the God of the universe grants.”
240.sharh: A report distinguishes special revelation from understanding God may grant a reader of scripture. The small written document mentioned in that exchange comes into view next.

translation: In your sheath was a curse on those who sacrificed
to anyone but my Lord. That reminder is enough for me.
241.sharh: The object in the sheath is a document. A transmitted version of its contents condemns making a sacrificial offering to anyone other than God.

translation: A sheet filled with light and knowledge,
rich in law and in the affirmation of God's oneness.
242.sharh: The small sheet holds teaching about conduct and worship. The repeated “in it” suggests more than this verse undertakes to list.

translation: You sent Abu al-Hayyaj out with orders,
orders the best of creation had dictated.
243.sharh: The instruction passes through two human relationships. Ali sends Abu al-Hayyaj on an assignment he says Muhammad had first given him.

translation: He carried out the order, effacing the image,
and levelling the graves where they had been raised.
244.sharh: This completes the reported commission. The hadith describes an image to be effaced and a conspicuously raised grave to be levelled.

translation: From you we know the standing of the two elders.
We preserve the report from your household through its chain.
245.sharh: Calling on a chain of transmitters is part of the argument. The poet wants the praise of the first two caliphs to be heard as testimony carried within Ali's own family.

translation: Through your cousin we trace the report back to you across the ages,
and also name your distinguished son whose mother came from Banu Hanifa.
246.sharh: Ali's son Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya bears a name taken from his mother’s tribe, Banu Hanifa. Bukhari records him asking his father about the standing of Abu Bakr and Umar.

translation: From you too we read the verses through unbroken transmission.
How favoured that community, how noble its teacher.
247.sharh: The chain now carries recitation itself. Successive teachers and pupils allow Ali's part in Quranic teaching to reach readers long after him.

translation: May victory in the next world bring you joy, Abu Hasan,
and may the Gardens of Eden rejoice in their good-hearted guest.
248.sharh: The blessing changes its recipient halfway through. Paradise itself is congratulated on the goodness of the man coming to it.

translation: Among a company that honoured its covenant and kept faith,
God, truest to his promise, will repay them with the best.
249.sharh: The same root serves both parties to the covenant. The people's fidelity is answered by a promise whose fulfilment is more certain still.

translation: Lover of the Commander of the Faithful, now
that you know the noble man's traits, imitate them.
250.sharh: The addressee changes one final time. The reader who has followed the biography is asked to reproduce something of its subject's conduct.

translation: For hostility to Ali, at its furthest extreme,
lies in opposing those qualities, scorning and belittling them.
251.sharh: Nasb is a historical term for hostility towards Ali. The poet sharpens it into a test of conduct for people who may profess to love him.

translation: A truth shining like the light of the sun.
Let whoever denies it deny the sun as much as he pleases.
252.sharh: The final image gives a visible form to the poet's conviction. The repeated sun leaves the denier speaking in the very light he disputes.

1.1.1.head: اِختال
1.1.1.meaning: To walk with a proud bearing.

1.1.6.head: تيه
1.1.6.meaning: Pride made visible in one's bearing.

1.2.6.head: تَنويه
1.2.6.meaning: Public praise that brings someone's merits to notice.

2.1.2-3.head: أَبو الحَسَنَين
2.1.2-3.meaning: Abu al-Hasanayn, father of Hasan and Husayn, a title of Ali.

2.1.4.head: النَّدب
2.1.4.meaning: One quick to answer a call for help, a man of courage and generosity.

2.2.4.head: حادٍ
2.2.4.meaning: A camel driver who urges the animals along with song.

3.1.5.head: حِقَب
3.1.5.meaning: Long ages or stretches of time.

5.2.5.head: جَدّ
5.2.5.meaning: To arise afresh or come to pass.

7.2.4.head: الأَقحاح
7.2.4.meaning: People regarded as speaking unmixed, native Arabic.

7.2.6.head: فوها
7.2.6.meaning: “Its mouth.” Here fi is the genitive of the noun for mouth, followed by a pronoun.

8.2.4.head: مَذاكٍ
8.2.4.meaning: Horses that have reached full strength and maturity.

9.1.3.head: المُختار
9.1.3.meaning: Al-Mukhtar, the Chosen One, a title of Muhammad.

9.2.1-2.head: تَحتَهُ امرَأَة
9.2.1-2.meaning: “His daughter is under you”, an older idiom for being married.

10.2.3.head: غالٍ
10.2.3.meaning: Someone who goes to excess in veneration.

10.2.4.head: قالٍ
10.2.4.meaning: Someone who bears hatred or aversion.

11.1.1-2.head: أَبو تُراب
11.1.1-2.meaning: Abu Turab, “father of dust”, a name Muhammad gave Ali on finding dust on him.

11.2.3.head: الأَثَر
11.2.3.meaning: Transmitted reports about earlier people and their words or conduct.

12.2.2.head: عِترَة
12.2.2.meaning: A person's close family, here Muhammad's household.

13.2.4.head: أَنأى
13.2.4.meaning: To draw apart or place at a distance.

14.2.3.head: صَرح
14.2.3.meaning: Lofty buildings that stand clear to view.

15.1.5.head: مَنقَبَة
15.1.5.meaning: A distinction or deed worthy of remembrance.

16.1.2.head: الحَسابَة
16.1.2.meaning: Standing reckoned from a family's distinctions.

17.1.6.head: سَمَق
17.1.6.meaning: To rise to a great height.

17.2.5.head: مَهوى
17.2.5.meaning: Drops or precipices into which one can fall.

20.2.1-2.head: بَطحاء مَكَّة
20.2.1-2.meaning: Batha' Makka, the gravelly level bed of the Meccan valley.

21.1.1.head: حاط
21.1.1.meaning: To shelter or guard someone against harm.

22.2.3.head: واتى
22.2.3.meaning: To accord with or favour something.

23.2.3-4.head: يَد بَيضاء
23.2.3-4.meaning: “A white hand”, a remembered act of generosity.

24.2.1-2.head: شَيبَة الحَمد
24.2.1-2.meaning: Shaybat al-Hamd, a name of Abd al-Muttalib, grandfather of Muhammad and Ali.

25.1.1.head: أَجَدّ
25.1.1.meaning: To renew, here to restore a well to use.

25.1.2.head: زَمزَم
25.1.2.meaning: Zamzam, the well near the Kaaba in Mecca.

25.1.5.head: كَوثَر
25.1.5.meaning: An abundance of good, here a plentiful supply of water.

26.1.2.head: أَبرَهَة
26.1.2.meaning: Abraha, the ruler in Yemen associated in Meccan tradition with the expedition of the Elephant.

27.1.2-3.head: عَمرو العُلى
27.1.2-3.meaning: Amr of the heights, a name for Hashim ibn Abd Manaf.

27.1.4-5.head: هَشّام أَرغِفَة
27.1.4-5.meaning: “Breaker of loaves”, evoking bread broken for a dish shared with guests.

27.2.2.head: راغِيَة
27.2.2.meaning: A she-camel described by the sound of its call.

28.2.1.head: إيلاف
28.2.1.meaning: Ilaf, an established arrangement or protection for trading journeys.

29.1.2.head: الرَّهط
29.1.2.meaning: A person's close kin or clan.

30.1.2-3.head: عَبد مَناف
30.1.2-3.meaning: Abd Manaf, Hashim's father and an ancestor of both Muhammad and Ali.

32.1.4.head: الإِنذار
32.1.4.meaning: The warning to the Prophet's nearest kindred in Quran 26:214.

33.1.2.head: زَيد
33.1.2.meaning: Zayd, the given name of Qusayy ibn Kilab.

34.1.2.head: خُزاعَة
34.1.2.meaning: Khuza'a, a tribe said in the Meccan tradition to have held custody of the sanctuary before Qusayy.

34.1.5.head: مُضَر
34.1.5.meaning: Mudar, an ancestor giving his name to a large group of northern Arab tribes.

35.1.3-4.head: سَدن البَيت
35.1.3-4.meaning: “Keeping the House”, custody of the Kaaba and its key.

35.2.2.head: الرِّفادَة
35.2.2.meaning: Rifada, the Meccan provision of food for pilgrims.

35.2.4.head: نادٍ
35.2.4.meaning: A council or meeting place, here associated with Mecca's Dar al-Nadwa.

36.1.3.head: كِلاب
36.1.3.meaning: Kilab ibn Murra, the ancestor at whom the Prophet's parental lines meet.

37.1.3.head: مُرَّة
37.1.3.meaning: Murra ibn Ka'b, the father of Kilab in the Quraysh genealogy.

37.1.5.head: كَعب
37.1.5.meaning: Ka'b ibn Lu'ayy, an ancestor of Quraysh.

38.1.4-5.head: أَمّا بَعد
38.1.4-5.meaning: “To proceed”, a transition from the opening of an address to its subject.

39.1.3.head: لُؤَيّ
39.1.3.meaning: Lu'ayy ibn Ghalib, father of Ka'b.

40.1.4.head: غالِب
40.1.4.meaning: Ghalib ibn Fihr, father of Lu'ayy.

40.2.1.head: سُمَيذَع
40.2.1.meaning: A magnanimous chief of high standing.

41.1.2.meaning: To outstrip or surpass one’s peers.

42.1.2.head: فِهر
42.1.2.meaning: Fihr ibn Malik, one of the ancestors proposed as the common forefather of Quraysh.

42.2.2.head: النَّضر
42.2.2.meaning: Al-Nadr ibn Kinana, Malik's father and another traditional common ancestor of Quraysh.

44.1.2.head: كِنانَة
44.1.2.meaning: Kinana ibn Khuzayma, both an ancestor's name and a tribal designation.

44.2.2.head: جُمجُمَة
44.2.2.meaning: A great parent tribe in genealogical usage.

45.1.2.head: خُزَيمَة
45.1.2.meaning: Khuzayma ibn Mudrika, father of Kinana in the genealogy.

45.1.5.head: مُدرِكَة
45.1.5.meaning: Mudrika ibn Ilyas, father of Khuzayma.

45.2.3.head: إِلياس
45.2.3.meaning: Ilyas ibn Mudar, an Arab ancestor distinct from the prophet of the same name.

46.1.6-7.head: مُضَر الحَمراء
46.1.6-7.meaning: Red Mudar, a traditional tribal designation. The article of “red” is divided from its noun by the metrical break.

47.1.2.head: نِزار
47.1.2.meaning: Nizar ibn Ma'add, father of Mudar.

48.1.2.head: مَعَدّ
48.1.2.meaning: Ma'add ibn Adnan, a forefather in the northern Arab genealogies.

48.1.4.head: عَدنان
48.1.4.meaning: Adnan, father of Ma'add and the last forefather named before Ishmael. His name does not usually take a final n in the genitive. Poetry permits the ending -in heard here.

48.2.5.head: عَفّى
48.2.5.meaning: To efface the traces of something.

49.1.4.head: مَحتِد
49.1.4.meaning: The stock or origin to which a lineage is traced.

49.2.5.head: إيهاً
49.2.5.meaning: “Enough, stop.” No one, the poet says, will silence their eulogist.

50.2.5.head: مَجانٍ
50.2.5.meaning: The fruits one gathers from the grove.

51.1.6.head: دِمَن
51.1.6.meaning: Accumulations of refuse and traces left on the ground.

52.1.4.head: أُكل
52.1.4.meaning: The produce or yield of cultivated land.

53.1.2.head: البَتول
53.1.2.meaning: Al-Batul, “the Chaste One”, a title of Fatima.

54.1.3.head: الأَشبال
54.1.3.meaning: Lion cubs, an image of youth.

55.1.1.head: الكِساء
55.1.1.meaning: Kisa', the cloak under which Muhammad gathered Ali, Fatima, Hasan and Husayn.

56.1.5.head: حَسَن
56.1.5.meaning: Hasan ibn Ali, the Prophet's grandson and Husayn's elder brother.

57.2.5.head: سَوافٍ
57.2.5.meaning: Winds that drive dust or sand before them.

58.1.3.head: قَرم
58.1.3.meaning: A foremost chief, originally a prized breeding camel.

59.1.1.head: نُبوءَة
59.1.1.meaning: A prophecy, here the prediction of Hasan's role in reconciling two Muslim parties.

60.1.2.head: الحُسَين
60.1.2.meaning: Husayn ibn Ali, the Prophet's grandson, killed at Karbala in 61 AH (680 CE).

61.2.4.head: أَلفى
61.2.4.meaning: To find or encounter. Husayn meets the same end that his father met.

62.1.7.head: غُرَر
62.1.7.meaning: Distinguished people, literally those marked by a bright blaze.

63.1.1.head: تَناوَش
63.1.1.meaning: To reach or assail from different directions.

64.2.6.head: جاثٍ
64.2.6.meaning: Someone kneeling or fallen to his knees.

65.1.2.head: زَينَب
65.1.2.meaning: Zaynab, daughter of Ali and Fatima and sister of Hasan and Husayn.

65.2.1-2.head: أُمّ كُلثوم
65.2.1-2.meaning: Umm Kulthum, the daughter of Ali and Fatima mentioned again in the marriage account.

66.1.2.head: العَقيلَة
66.1.2.meaning: A woman esteemed and cherished by her family.

67.1.3-4.head: بَحر الجود
67.1.3-4.meaning: “Sea of generosity”, Abd Allah ibn Ja'far, Zaynab's husband, celebrated for liberality.

67.2.3.head: الفاروق
67.2.3.meaning: Al-Faruq, a title of Umar ibn al-Khattab, the second caliph.

68.1.3.head: أَصهَر
68.1.3.meaning: To become related to a family through marriage.

70.1.5.head: العَبّاس
70.1.5.meaning: Al-Abbas ibn Ali. The conjunction and article precede the break, and his name resumes in the next half.

71.2.2.head: صاغِيَة
71.2.2.meaning: A person's inner circle of loyal supporters.

72.1.2.head: عُبَيد
72.1.2.meaning: Ubayd, named beside Abd Allah. Genealogies of Ali's children also give the name Ubayd Allah.

73.1.4-6.head: قَضى نَحبَه
73.1.4-6.meaning: “Fulfilled their term”, a Quranic expression associated here with death.

74.1.5.head: بَخٍ
74.1.5.meaning: “How fine”, an expression of admiration, doubled across the two halves.

75.1.2.head: حِلس
75.1.2.meaning: A cloth kept close under a saddle, hence an inseparable companion.

76.1.5.head: مُعتَرَك
76.1.5.meaning: A place of encounter or struggle.

77.2.5.head: تالٍ
77.2.5.meaning: What follows this life, the hereafter.

78.2.2.head: الثَّلاثَة
78.2.2.meaning: The three apparently evoked are Khadija, Abu Bakr and Zayd ibn Haritha, all named among the earliest believers.

80.1.4.head: عُهدَة
80.1.4.meaning: A charge committed to someone's care, here associated with returning deposits.

81.1.5.head: عَجَل
81.1.5.meaning: Haste. The final consonant sounds closer to r in the recitation. The card reads ajal, which fits the hurried reunion.

81.2.2.head: الفَواطِم
81.2.2.meaning: Al-Fawatim, “the Fatimas”, women sharing one name, including the Prophet's daughter in the migration accounts.

82.2.3.head: البَضعَة
82.2.3.meaning: A piece of flesh, alluding to Muhammad's description of Fatima as part of himself.

83.2.1.head: قَبَس
83.2.1.meaning: To take a flame from another fire, here to receive guidance.

85.1.2.head: تَبوك
85.1.2.meaning: Tabuk, north of Medina, the destination of the expedition of 9 AH (630 CE).

85.1.4.head: طابَة
85.1.4.meaning: Taba, a traditional name of Medina. The verse extends the final vowel.

86.1.4.head: هارون
86.1.4.meaning: Aaron, brother of Moses and the figure in the comparison traditionally addressed to Ali.

86.2.2.head: الكَليم
86.2.2.meaning: Al-Kalim, “the one God spoke to”, an epithet of Moses. Aaron was his brother.

87.2.2.head: العُهود
87.2.2.meaning: The treaties addressed in the opening of Quran 9.

88.2.3.head: العَضباء
88.2.3.meaning: Al-Adba', the name of one of Muhammad's riding camels.

89.1.3.head: جَمع
89.1.3.meaning: A gathering. Jam' is also a name for Muzdalifa, though the verse itself describes an assembled audience.

90.1.1.head: بَراءَة
90.1.1.meaning: Bara'a, disavowal, the opening word and an alternative name of Quran 9.

91.1.2.head: الغَدير
91.1.2.meaning: Ghadir Khumm, a watering place between Mecca and Medina associated with Muhammad's declaration about Ali.

91.2.5.head: تَوَلٍّ
91.2.5.meaning: To give loyalty and support to the Prophet's family.

92.2.4.head: مِشكاة
92.2.4.meaning: A niche for a lamp, evoking the image in Quran 24:35.

94.2.3.head: الفِردَوس
94.2.3.meaning: Firdaws, Paradise or its loftiest garden.

95.1.4.head: اللَّحد
95.1.4.meaning: The lateral burial niche cut into the side of a grave.

96.1.2.head: بَدر
96.1.2.meaning: Badr, the site of the encounter between the Medinan Muslims and Quraysh in 2 AH (624 CE).

97.1.1.head: زامَل
97.1.1.meaning: To share a mount or travel as someone's riding companion.

97.1.5.head: عَقَب
97.1.5.meaning: To succeed another rider in taking a turn.

99.1.3-4.head: عَبد الدّار
99.1.3-4.meaning: Abd al-Dar, the Quraysh clan associated with bearing the standard.

99.1.7.head: اللِّواء
99.1.7.meaning: The article of al-liwa', the standard, joins the rest of its word across the pause.

100.1.2.head: سَخينَة
100.1.2.meaning: Sakhina, a derisive nickname for Quraysh, originally the name of a dish.

101.1.2.meaning: “Come down and fight”, a challenge to single combat.

102.1.1-2.head: هَذانِ خَصمان
102.1.1-2.meaning: “These two are adversaries”, the opening of Quran 22:19, linked in hadith to the champions at Badr.

103.1.3.head: الأَحزاب
103.1.3.meaning: Al-Ahzab, the confederates who besieged Medina at the Trench.

104.1.4.head: اِرتَجَز
104.1.4.meaning: Chanting rajaz, a verse metre often used for challenges and boasts.

104.2.1-3.head: عَمرو بن وُدّ
104.2.1-3.meaning: Amr ibn Abd Wudd, the Qurayshi horseman who fought Ali at the Trench in Ibn Ishaq’s account. The poet shortens his name to Amr ibn Wudd.
